opus-5.5.text:
I think what really drew me in was that the game felt *alive* in a way other games didn't. In most games I played as a kid, everything was scripted: you press a button, a predetermined animation plays. But in something like Crazy Machines, you set up a few pieces, a ball, a ramp, some dominoes, and then you just let go and watch what happens. The outcome wasn't written by a designer line by line; it emerged from the rules of physics. That felt magical to me.

There was also this sense of creativity and freedom. There wasn't just one correct solution. You could try something weird, and sometimes it would work in a way nobody expected. That loop of experimenting, failing, adjusting, and finally seeing the whole chain reaction succeed was incredibly satisfying.

When I started trying to make little games myself, I quickly ran into the question: how does the computer actually *know* how a ball should bounce or how a stack of boxes should fall? That curiosity, wanting to understand what was going on under the hood, ended up being far more interesting to me than the games themselves. I started reading about numerical integration, collision detection, and so on, and I think that's really where my long-term interest in physical simulation and computer graphics began. In a way, those simple physics games were my gateway into everything I've worked on since.

r002.rationale: The response says Crazy Machines appealed because outcomes emerged from physics rules, explicitly linking his interest in the game to physics simulation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, what hooked me about Crazy Machines was that the game wasn't really about winning in the usual sense. You're given this box of gears, balls, candles, balloons, ropes, and a goal like "get the ball into the basket," and the fun was entirely in watching the chain reaction unfold. You press play and the world just obeys physical rules. Sometimes it did exactly what you planned, and sometimes it did something completely unexpected, and the unexpected part was often more delightful.

As a kid I didn't have the vocabulary for it, but what I was really enjoying was simulation. The game was a little physics engine, and I was poking at it to see what it could do. That feeling of "I set up the initial conditions, and then the computer tells me what happens next" is addictive. It's the same feeling I get now when I run a fluid simulation and see water splash in a way I didn't fully predict.

So when I started making my own games, I wanted that. I didn't want to hand-animate every outcome. I wanted to build a small world with rules and let the player discover things inside it. Rigid bodies, springs, collisions, that kind of thing. It's also just a very honest way to build a game: if the physics is right, the gameplay tends to feel right, and players trust it.

And practically speaking, it was a great excuse to learn how simulation actually works under the hood. Writing a physics engine for a game forces you to confront integration schemes, stability, collision detection, performance, all of that. I didn't realize at the time that I was basically training myself for the research I'd end up doing later. Looking back, Crazy Machines planted the seed, and everything after was me trying to build bigger and faster machines.

When I started making games, I was drawn to that idea: you define a few physical rules, and those rules let players come up with all kinds of creative solutions.
